common_meaning: Used to make a request polite; also to make someone happy or satisfied.
example: Please close the door; nothing pleased him more than a quiet morning.
rrgm_bridge: Please softens a request by acknowledging that the other person could say no.
invariant_mi: A politeness marker on requests; or to give satisfaction.

domain_entries.REL: Marks a request as a request rather than a command, leaving room for refusal.
domain_entries.LIN: Politeness particle; "if you please" and "as you please" leave the choice with the other.
domain_entries.AFF: To please someone is to bring them satisfaction. Provisional domain.

count_condition: A request addressed to someone able to decline it, or an act that satisfies someone.
transfer_boundary: Saying please does not turn a command into a free choice when the speaker has power over the listener. Trying to please others is not the same as caring for them; it can mean avoiding honest disagreement.

common_meaning: To move something into a place or position; also to express in words, or bring into a state.
example: Put the bowl on the shelf; let me put it another way.
rrgm_bridge: Put places something somewhere by an act: the thing ends up where the actor set it.
invariant_mi: To cause something to be in a place, form or state.

domain_entries.PHY: Moving an object to a position.
domain_entries.LIN: Very productive in phrasal verbs (put off, put up with, put out), whose meanings often can't be guessed from the parts.

count_condition: An actor causing an object, idea or person to be in a place, wording or condition.
transfer_boundary: Phrasal uses differ sharply: "put up" a shelf, "put up with" noise, "put someone up" for the night. Putting a claim into words does not make it true.

common_meaning: A social gathering of invited guests, typically with food, drink and entertainment.
example: We're having a party for her birthday on Saturday.
rrgm_bridge: A party gathers people around a shared occasion; the gathering is the point.
invariant_mi: A gathering of people for celebration or enjoyment.

domain_entries.REL: Parties mark occasions and strengthen ties; who is invited also draws a line around a group.
domain_entries.AFF: Associated with celebration and enjoyment, though not everyone finds them enjoyable. Provisional domain.

count_condition: People gathered for a social occasion.
transfer_boundary: Being at a party is not the same as enjoying it. An invitation list includes some people and leaves others out.

common_meaning: An organised group of people with shared political aims who seek to win elections and hold power.
example: The two main parties both promised lower taxes.
rrgm_bridge: A political party bundles many positions into one platform so that voters can choose between them.
invariant_mi: An organisation that competes for political power on a shared platform.

domain_entries.REL: Parties organise coalitions of interests; party loyalty can bind members to positions they would not all hold alone.
domain_entries.ECO: Parties raise money and compete for votes.

count_condition: An organised group contesting elections or holding power on a shared programme.
transfer_boundary: A party's platform is not every member's view. Agreeing with a party on one issue does not mean agreeing on all.

sense_label: one side in an agreement or dispute
common_meaning: A person or group taking part in a contract, legal case or dispute.
example: Both parties signed the agreement.
rrgm_bridge: A party is one side of a structured relation: an agreement, a case, a conversation.
invariant_mi: One of the participants in a defined relation such as a contract or dispute.

domain_entries.REL: Each party has rights and obligations within the relation.
domain_entries.FOR: In law and logic, the identified sides whose positions are compared.

count_condition: A participant identified as one side of an agreement, case or exchange.
transfer_boundary: Being a party to something means being involved in it, not necessarily agreeing to all of it; third parties are outside the relation but may be affected by it.

common_meaning: The elected head of a republic; also the head of a company, university, club or organisation.
example: The president signed the bill; she became president of the chess club.
rrgm_bridge: A president holds the top office of a structure for a term, under rules that define and limit the role.
invariant_mi: The holder of the highest office in a state or organisation, for a set term or until replaced.

domain_entries.REL: Authority is granted by election or appointment, and limited by constitutions, boards or members.
domain_entries.ECO: In companies, the president often runs operations, under a board.

count_condition: A person holding the chief office of a republic or organisation.
transfer_boundary: The office and the person are separate: the office's powers come from its rules, not from the person. The title means different things in different organisations.

common_meaning: Letters and parcels sent by mail; also a message or piece of content published online. As a verb, to send by mail or to publish.
example: The parcel came in the post; she posted a photo of the sunset.
rrgm_bridge: A post is a message released into a channel, where it travels to readers the sender may never see.
invariant_mi: A message or item sent or published for others to receive.

domain_entries.DIG: Online posts on social media and forums; posting makes content public or semi-public, often permanently.
domain_entries.REL: What is posted can be read out of context and by people the writer did not have in mind.

count_condition: An item or message sent by mail or published to a channel.
transfer_boundary: Deleting a post does not guarantee it is gone; copies may remain. A post's reach is not the same as its accuracy.

common_meaning: A job or official position; also an upright pole fixed in the ground.
example: She took up a post at the embassy; the fence post leaned in the wind.
rrgm_bridge: Both senses name a fixed point: a pole set in the ground, or a role someone is stationed in.
invariant_mi: A fixed upright support, or an assigned position or job.

domain_entries.REL: An official post carries duties and authority tied to the role.
domain_entries.PHY: An upright support carrying load to the ground.

count_condition: A pole fixed upright, or a role or station assigned to someone.
transfer_boundary: Holding a post confers the role's authority, not personal authority beyond it.

common_meaning: Attractive in a delicate or pleasing way; also (as an adverb) fairly or quite.
example: It's a pretty village; the test was pretty hard.
rrgm_bridge: Pretty grades two things lightly: appearance as pleasing, and degree as "more than a little".
invariant_mi: Pleasing in appearance; or, as an adverb, to a moderate degree.

domain_entries.LIN: As an adverb, a common hedge meaning "fairly", which can soften or intensify depending on tone.
domain_entries.AFF: Aesthetic appreciation of something pleasing to look at. Provisional domain.

count_condition: Something judged pleasing to look at, or a degree marked as moderate.
transfer_boundary: "Pretty sure" is less than sure. Judgements of prettiness vary between people and cultures.

common_meaning: Very likely; more likely than not.
example: It will probably rain this afternoon.
rrgm_bridge: Probably leans toward a claim without fully committing; it puts the weight on one side but leaves the other open.
invariant_mi: Marks a proposition as more likely true than false.

domain_entries.COG: Expresses an estimate of likelihood above even odds.
domain_entries.FOR: Informally maps to a probability above 0.5, though people use it for a wide range of confidence.

count_condition: A claim the speaker judges more likely than not.
transfer_boundary: Probably is an estimate, not a fact; the speaker's calibration matters. A probable outcome can still fail to happen.

common_meaning: The time before the present, and the events in it; also gone by, or (as a preposition) beyond or after.
example: In the past, the village had a school; we walked past the station; it's ten past six.
rrgm_bridge: The past is what has already been written into the record; it can be reinterpreted but not undone.
invariant_mi: Prior to the present, or beyond a point in time or space.

domain_entries.PHY: Earlier along the direction of time; the arrow of time runs from past to future.
domain_entries.REL: Shared pasts shape relationships; someone's past is part of their record without being the whole of them.
domain_entries.LIN: The past tense marks completed or earlier action.

count_condition: A time or event before the present, or a point that has been passed.
transfer_boundary: The past is fixed as event but open as interpretation: what happened stays, while what it means can be revised. Someone's past does not decide their present.

common_meaning: The official body responsible for keeping public order, preventing crime and enforcing the law; also its members.
example: The police closed the road after the accident.
rrgm_bridge: The police are the part of a state's structure authorised to use force to uphold its laws, under rules that limit that force.
invariant_mi: The civil force authorised to enforce law and maintain order.

domain_entries.REL: Public trust in police depends on accountability; who oversees the police is a recurring question.
domain_entries.FOR: Police powers are set and limited by law, including rules on arrest, search and evidence.

count_condition: An authorised public body enforcing law, or its officers.
transfer_boundary: Police enforce the law; they do not decide guilt, which is for courts. Authority to use force is limited by law and is not the same as being right in a given case.

common_meaning: A telephone, especially a mobile phone; as a verb, to call someone by telephone.
example: I'll phone you when I land; my phone is almost out of battery.
rrgm_bridge: A phone carries a voice across distance, and the mobile phone carries a whole networked life in one pocket.
invariant_mi: A device for voice communication at a distance, now usually a networked handheld computer.

domain_entries.DIG: Smartphones are computers with apps, data, location and constant connection.
domain_entries.REL: Phones keep people reachable, which can connect them and also blur the line between work and rest.
domain_entries.PHY: Converts sound to electrical or radio signals and back.

count_condition: A device used for remote voice communication, or the act of calling.
transfer_boundary: Being reachable is not the same as being available. A phone holds a great deal of personal data; access to it is access to much of a life.

common_meaning: A person taking part in a game or sport; also someone who plays a musical instrument; also a device that plays recordings.
example: Each player gets seven cards; she's a fine cello player.
rrgm_bridge: A player acts within a game's rules; the rules define which moves count.
invariant_mi: A participant in a game, performance or playing activity, or a device that plays media.

domain_entries.REL: "A key player" is someone with influence in a situation; informally, "player" can also mean someone who plays with others' affections.
domain_entries.FOR: In game theory, a decision-maker whose choices affect outcomes for others.
domain_entries.DIG: Media players are programs or devices that play audio or video.

count_condition: A participant acting within a game or performance, or a device that plays media.
transfer_boundary: Calling someone a player in a situation describes influence, not intent. The game-theory sense assumes rational choices, which real people do not always make.

common_meaning: Relating to government, public affairs or the contest for power; also relating to power relations within any group.
example: The decision was more political than practical.
rrgm_bridge: Political names whatever involves who decides for a group and how that power is won and checked.
invariant_mi: Concerning the distribution and exercise of power in a group or state.

domain_entries.REL: Office politics and family politics use the same word for power relations at smaller scales.
domain_entries.ECO: Political decisions shape budgets, markets and regulation.

count_condition: A matter involving government or the exercise of power in a group.
transfer_boundary: Calling something political can be used to dismiss it ("that's just political") without addressing its merits. Nearly every public decision has a political side; that does not make it only political.

common_meaning: The amount of money expected or paid for something; also what must be given up to get something.
example: The price of bread has gone up; fame came at a price.
rrgm_bridge: A price is the measure an exchange sets: what one side gives up so the other will let go.
invariant_mi: The amount exchanged for a good or service, or the cost of gaining something.

domain_entries.ECO: Prices respond to supply and demand, costs and market power.
domain_entries.REL: "The price" of a choice can be paid by others than the one who chose.

count_condition: A stated or paid amount in exchange, or a cost borne for an outcome.
transfer_boundary: Price is not value: something cheap can be precious, and something expensive can be worthless to a given person.

common_meaning: A planned piece of work with a particular aim; as a verb, to estimate, to throw forward, or to display an image on a surface.
example: The project will take two years; they projected a map onto the wall.
rrgm_bridge: A project casts an intended future and organises work toward it.
invariant_mi: A planned undertaking toward a goal, or to cast forward.

domain_entries.ECO: Projects have budgets, timelines and deliverables.
domain_entries.COG: Psychological projection: attributing one's own feelings or traits to others.
domain_entries.PHY: Projecting light or an image onto a surface.

count_condition: A planned undertaking, or an act of casting forward or estimating.
transfer_boundary: A projection is an estimate, not a fact. Projection in psychology is a claim about a mind, which should be made carefully.

common_meaning: A length of time; also a full stop in punctuation; also menstruation.
example: The museum is closed for a short period; put a period at the end of the sentence.
rrgm_bridge: A period is a bounded span: of time, of a sentence, of a cycle.
invariant_mi: A bounded interval, or a mark that ends a sentence.

domain_entries.PHY: The time taken for one cycle of a repeating motion.
domain_entries.BIO: Menstruation, part of the monthly cycle.
domain_entries.LIN: The full stop; "period" used for emphasis to end an argument.

count_condition: An interval of time, the end of a sentence, or a menstrual cycle phase.
transfer_boundary: Saying "period" to end an argument signals finality, not that the argument is settled.

common_meaning: Having no faults; complete; exactly right for a purpose.
example: The weather was perfect for a picnic.
rrgm_bridge: Perfect names a state with nothing left to fix, which is more often a judgement than a measurement.
invariant_mi: Without flaw, or fully suited to a purpose.

domain_entries.FOR: In mathematics, a perfect number equals the sum of its divisors.
domain_entries.LIN: The perfect tense marks completed action ("I have finished").
domain_entries.COG: Perfectionism is a demand for flawlessness that can block finishing anything.

count_condition: Something judged flawless or entirely fit for a purpose.
transfer_boundary: "Perfect" in everyday speech usually means very good, not flawless. A standard of perfection that nothing can meet is a way of moving the line.

common_meaning: A public green area for recreation; as a verb, to leave a vehicle somewhere for a time.
example: We had lunch in the park; you can park on the street.
rrgm_bridge: A park is land held open for everyone to use; to park is to set something down and leave it waiting.
invariant_mi: A public recreational area, or to leave a vehicle stationary.

domain_entries.ECO: Public parks are shared goods maintained from public funds.
domain_entries.REL: Parks give shared space where strangers meet.

count_condition: A public green space, or the act of leaving a vehicle.
transfer_boundary: Parking an issue sets it aside; it does not resolve it.

common_meaning: The act of presenting a play, concert or other entertainment; also how well a person or thing does something.
example: The performance ended with a standing ovation; the car's performance improved.
rrgm_bridge: Performance is doing something before an audience or a measure, so that it can be seen and judged.
invariant_mi: The carrying out of an act, or how well it is done.

domain_entries.REL: Social performance: people present themselves differently in different settings, which is not the same as being false.
domain_entries.ECO: Performance reviews measure work against targets.
domain_entries.DIG: System performance: speed, throughput and reliability.

count_condition: An act carried out before observers, or its measured effectiveness.
transfer_boundary: Calling something "just a performance" can dismiss it unfairly; performance and sincerity are not opposites. A measured performance depends on what was measured.

common_meaning: To push steadily against something; also newspapers and journalists collectively; also a machine for pressing or printing.
example: Press the button; the press gathered outside the court.
rrgm_bridge: To press is to apply steady force; the press applies public attention.
invariant_mi: To exert steady force, or the news media collectively.

domain_entries.PHY: Pressure: force applied over an area.
domain_entries.REL: A free press holds power to account; press coverage shapes public views.

count_condition: An act of pushing, or the institutions of journalism.
transfer_boundary: Being "pressed" for an answer is pressure, not evidence; an answer given under pressure tells you about the pressure as well as the answer.

common_meaning: The process of making or growing something; also the amount made; also a play, film or show as staged.
example: Production fell during the strike; a new production of Hamlet.
rrgm_bridge: Production turns inputs into outputs through work.
invariant_mi: The making of goods or works, or what is made.

domain_entries.ECO: Output of goods; production costs and capacity.
domain_entries.DIG: "In production" names a system live for real users, as opposed to testing.

count_condition: A process of making, its output, or a staged work.
transfer_boundary: High production is not high value; output can grow while quality falls.
